articles.headline: How long will humans be needed for translation?
keyFacts: Google said people translate one trillion words monthly on Google Translate, amid growing industry adoption of AI translation tools.
Translators warn that AI translation still produces critical errors in legal and medical fields despite sounding natural and fluent.
Researcher François Yvon expects future AI translation systems will evaluate their own work and indicate when they are not sure.
body: - Published
"Il pleut des cordes," say the French when it's raining hard.
"It's raining ropes," is the direct translation. It's the kind of idiom which can trip up an AI translator.
"You can imagine the dilemma this throws AI into," says FranÃ§ois Yvon, a research director specialised in automatic translation with the French National Centre for Scientific Research CNRS.
He says a well-trained system will know that ropes are not literally falling from the sky and use the English phrase "it's raining cats and dogs".
"But is it going to find the equivalent when it's translating into Indonesian?" asks Yvon.
A comment on the weather is pretty low-risk, but more and more translation is being done by machines, and on topics with higher stakes than the weather.
In April, Google said people are now translating, external one trillion words a month with Google Translate.
That doesn't count the others: DeepL, Microsoft, Claude, ChatCGT and Gemini, not to mention made-to-measure corporate translation systems.
Direct sales of machine translation, external (i.e. outside general AI subscriptions) were worth an estimated $1.4bn (Â£1bn) last year.

"For plenty of use cases, raw AI translation is now the right call: multiplying your costs by 100 to catch the last few percent of errors isn't rational if you're translating internal documents or product listings," says John Zimmerman, founder of OKA (Open Knowledge Association), a Swiss non-profit that translates Wikipedia articles into other languages.
"For an encyclopedia it's different. Wikipedia runs on trust. A wrong fact can sit there for years and get cited by journalists and AI systems," he says.

With more than 10,000 published pieces, mostly into Spanish, Portuguese and English, OKA is, Zimmerman says, the single largest contributor of translated articles to the collaborative online encyclopedia.
Which is something it absolutely could not have become without AI.
"Translating 10,000 articles the traditional way would cost millions. In our process, the AI produces the draft, then a human translator checks every sentence," he explains.
But that human input is required less and less.

"The machine output is now good enough that skipping the human entirely has become a serious option, and a real temptation across the industry. Two or three years ago, with tools like DeepL, our translators still rewrote a good chunk of every draft.
"Today the prose often doesn't need fixing at all. So, the question is no longer whether AI translation is good, it clearly is, but whether it's good enough to remove the human," says Zimmerman.
Not yet, translators argue.
Ariella BaltiÃ© is a translator and legal expert specialised in translating court documents from English into French.
She was contacted recently by someone who'd already translated his documents with AI, asking her to check them.
"There were two major errors right at the beginning," she said.
The AI had translated "Le demandeur" (the plaintiff) as "the requester". "Totally awkward for legal papers," says BaltiÃ©.
When the AI saw "Madame X, Ã©pouse Y" (Ms X, wife of Y'), it came up with "Ms X marries Y".
In other words, it mistook a noun for a verb, completely losing the meaning of the phrase.
The consequences of mistranslation in the legal sphere can be serious. In the US, for example, errors in machine-translated asylum applications have led to delays in the release of detainees.
Accuracy is a matter of life and death in the medical field.
"The units for dosages and blood tests often include Greek letters," says Carol Bereuter, who is a specialist in medical translations.
She came across one automatically-translated text that had translated the greek letter Î¼ as milli (one thousandth) instead of micro (one millionth).
"That's a serious error. If you give someone a milligram when it's meant to be a microgram, you are giving them a thousand times the dose," points out Bereuter.
She also makes the point that, as AI translators have got better, catching errors has got more difficult.

"Whereas in the past, with things like Google Translate, the sentence would jump out at you because there'd be a grammatical error or it would sound clunky, today it sounds perfectly legitimate. It sounds fluid. It sounds natural. So the errors are a lot harder to spot."

"If it's something that will bear your signature, there's a risk for your reputation. And if decisions are going to be taken on the basis of a translation concerning a medical procedure, a contract you might sign or a major purchase you might make, the risk is even greater," warns FranÃ§ois Yvon.
Even sentences that seem quite clear to a human can trip up an AI service, he says.

"When you have words with different meanings, it's usually very clear for a human which one applies because they understand the context, but when a machine translator comes across the sentence 'translate into Polish', for example, it is quite capable of deciding it must be all about shoe cream, says Yvon.
Context is often crucial. If an AI translator hasn't grasped that we're talking about a football match it is liable to mis-translate "taking a corner".
Last year OKA ran a study, funded by Wikimedia. It studied 119 articles, 10 language pairs and more than 1,000 hours of translator work.

"27% of the AI-generated text still got corrected before publication. Three quarters of those corrections were errors the AI introduced, and 5 to 6% of errors changed the meaning of the original text," says Zimmerman.
Eradicating those errors is likely to be challenging.
"As things stand, I think the fundamental way these systems function makes it quite hard to imagine how they could become 100% reliable," says FranÃ§ois Yvon.

This is because probability is a crucial part of the way AI translates each word rather than another and what is probably correct is not the same as what is correct. Especially in the realm of something as subtle and surprising as language.
He thinks a new generation of tech will be an improvement.

"We will see translation systems that are increasingly capable of evaluating what they do and correcting themselves using different AI tools simultaneously: one to do the translation, a second to criticize it and a third to produce a new version, for example."
But perhaps the big moment will be when AI can show doubt.
"The real breakthrough won't come until these systems are not merely capable of translating but also of telling us when they're not sure," Yvon says.

articles.headline: Saka responds to Arteta's challenge with 'huge impact'
keyFacts: Bukayo Saka came off the bench despite illness to score a goal and provide an assist in Arsenal's 3-0 Champions League win over Lille.
Arsenal manager Mikel Arteta stated before the match that he wants Saka to aim for two or three goals per game.
Arteta said that Saka delivered a huge impact with real quality in response to the scoring challenge set for him.
body: - Published
Bukayo Saka responded to the challenge set by Arsenal manager Mikel Arteta as he proved a game-changer in the 3-0 Champions League win over Lille.
The England forward has been told he should aim to score "two or three" goals per game - such was his quality and the expectation from his boss.
Saka did not achieve that tally against the French visitors, but shook off illness to come off the bench and assist Eberechi Eze's strike that made it 2-0, before rolling in his side's third goal.
The 25-year-old has now scored four goals in nine games this season and looks to be taking the next step in his evolution as Arsenal's key man.

With the majority of his side's attacking play involving him, he has always been an influential figure. But with opposition defenders doubling up on him and injury issues over the last two seasons, there were doubts over whether Saka could still do what was asked of him in attack or if he had lost a yard of pace.
Arteta has tweaked Saka's positioning this season and, prior to Lille's visit, said it has been done deliberately to get him closer to the goal.
'He delivered with real quality'

"That is where we need to get him," said the Gunners boss before the game. "And if he misses the chance, so be it. At the end, the more volume we generate, the bigger the probability of him scoring more goals."
Saka's strike against Lille was a confident one-touch finish and came after he missed a late one-on-one opportunity in Saturday's Premier League victory over Leeds.
"He has been getting in great positions, getting shots, getting one-touch finishes and tap-ins," added Arteta.

"That is the kind of unpredictability we have with that player, otherwise we know how the opponent is going to defend him. He is doing well, he could have had another four or five goals by now, easily. But if he continues like that, we know.

"When he talks about scoring a certain amount of goals, he needs to be thinking about scoring a certain amount of goals per game. If that shifts, that mentality, he will get into those positions and score more goals."
Saka has scored 20 goals in a season just once in his career, which came in the 2023-24 campaign and 16 in the Premier League.

But the winger has also been in good goalscoring form for England with five in his last four matches and scored a double in the 7-0 Nations League demolition of Croatia in the recent international break.

Saka is now on 19 goals in major European competitions for Arsenal, only behind Thierry Henry (42), while he has nine assists in the Champions League which puts him behind Henry (16) and Cesc Fabregas (14).
He has refused to disclose the targets he has set himself, but Arteta welcomed Saka's response following his message to do more in front of goal.
The Spaniard said: "I don't know if that's the case, but I am very happy.

"He wasn't feeling that good yesterday and today, as he had some sort of illness. He wasn't ready to start but he was really wanting to contribute to the team if it was needed and he came on and made a huge impact and delivered with real quality."
Arteta revealed he also spoke to Saka after telling the media about his desire for the player to have a greater impact.
"After the press conference... I said 'Bukayo, I just killed you in the press conference, good luck tomorrow'.
"He was laughing. He knows that we have discussed these kind of things and he takes it because he wants to be the best version of himself.
"In order to do that, you have to put big objectives and challenges and try to reason by working and being consistent - and when it doesn't work, keep going because he has the ability to do it."
Gyokeres struggles on mixed night for fringe players
Arteta made five changes to the team that started the win over Leeds as the Gunners looked to navigate six matches in all competitions during this month.
Noni Madueke moved to the right wing after putting in a good performance on the left at the weekend, with Mikel Merino, Eze and Viktor Gyokeres all coming into the starting XI.
Eze had started just two games in all competitions before the match with Lille and Arteta had said his attitude had been "phenomenal" despite a lack of game time.
The 28-year-old showed flashes of his undoubted quality and his finish for Arsenal's second goal - and his first of the season - will give him confidence going forward.
Madueke had a mixed night as he showed his ability to beat a defender, but questions remain over his end product - even if he provided the assist for Jurrien Timber's classy opening goal.
However, it was not a good night for Gyokeres.
The Sweden striker scored 21 goals in all competitions last season as Arsenal won the title for the first time in 22 years and displayed his willingness to run and work hard.
But Gyokeres had just 12 touches before being replaced and Kai Havertz, as he so often does, looked a much better and more natural fit for the Arsenal frontline, teeing up Saka's goal too.

Arteta brought on Saka, Havertz and Martin Odegaard after going 1-0 up and all three contributed to show why they are still the first names on the teamsheet and why the Arsenal boss will be so reliant on them if they are to achieve more honours.

articles.headline: Martin Shkreli livestreamed himself violating lifetime pharma ban, FTC says
keyFacts: The FTC and seven states asked a federal judge to hold Martin Shkreli in contempt for allegedly violating his lifetime pharmaceutical industry ban.
Officials alleged that Shkreli violated the ban by trading drug company stocks and discussing the industry during social media livestreams.
Regulators asked the court to make Shkreli divest his pharmaceutical stocks, forfeit trading profits, and face escalating future consequences.
body: Martin Shkreli—the ex-pharmaceutical executive infamous for illegally hiking the price of a lifesaving anti-parasitic drug by more than 4,000 percent and getting a seven-year prison sentence for the fraudulent scheme he used to do it—has been under a lifetime ban from the pharmaceutical industry since 2022.

However, according to the Federal Trade Commission and the attorneys general of seven states, Shkreli has “flagrantly and repeatedly” violated that ban nearly the entire time—allegedly by trading stock in dozens of drug companies and discussing the industry during livestreams on social media.

On Tuesday, the FTC and the seven states asked a federal judge to hold Shkreli in contempt for the alleged violations. The states include New York, California, Illinois, North Carolina, Ohio, Pennsylvania, and Virginia—the same states that joined the FTC in suing Shkreli in 2020 over the “elaborate anticompetitive scheme” involving the anti-parasitic drug, Daraprim. The scheme raised the price from $17.50 per pill to $750 per pill virtually overnight, while blocking generic competitors from entering the market.
“Egregious” conduct

In 2022, the federal court recognized the “seriousness” of issuing such a lifetime industry ban, but ruled that “Shkreli’s egregious, deliberate, repetitive, long-running, and ultimately dangerous illegal conduct warrants imposition of an injunction of this scope.” The ban, among many things, “explicitly prohibits” Shkreli from owning stock in pharmaceutical companies and making public statements that could influence a pharmaceutical company’s business, according to the FTC and the states.

With the alleged violations, the FTC and the states are now seeking to force Shkreli to divest from all pharmaceutical companies and pay a fine equal to his profits from trading pharmaceutical company stocks. They also want the court to lay out “clear and escalating consequences” if Shkreli violates the ban in the future, including further financial penalties and incarceration.

articles.headline: Anthropic reinvents source control as Claude floods the world with code
keyFacts: Anthropic said its Claude models increased merged code changes from 2,500 per day in May 2026 to over 30,000 per day by September.
Anthropic stated that this exponential growth overwhelmed its coding infrastructure and forced the company to build a centralized version control system called Scion.
Anthropic reported that Scion and other custom infrastructure tools were created with assistance from Claude models to manage massive AI-generated code volumes.
body: Anthropic's Claude models have been emitting so much code that the company's coding infrastructure hasn't been able to keep up. It's a symptom of the AI coding imperative and all-you-can-eat inference. Microsoft's GitHub in April published a blog post attributing recent availability problems to the exponential growth in pull requests and commits. The code flood has been noted by academic researchers, among others. For Anthropic, writing code is no longer a productivity bottleneck. Instead, the problem is managing the code after it's written, via source control, the build system, and continuous integration. "In May 2026, Anthropic averaged around 2,500 code changes merged per day; as of September, we merged over 30,000 per day," the biz said in a blog post on Tuesday. "We don’t expect this rate of growth to slow down anytime soon; the latent demand for merging code is practically infinite, and every bottleneck we remove immediately leads to a further increase in the amount of code we produce." After several months of model prompting and five months of migration, the result is a homemade version control system called Scion, a monorepo scheme that sounds a bit like Subversion, Apache's centralized version control system. Anthropic is not the first organization to look beyond Git's distributed architecture toward centralized source control. Google uses Piper, a monorepo system (along with Gerrit for Git-based code reviews). Microsoft has Virtual File System for Git, formerly GVFS, to help overcome some of the scaling issues with Git. Meta has Sapling. But as the AI biz notes, Claude's code writing ability both created the situation and offered a way out through the creation of scalable code infrastructure tools – in addition to Scion, Claude helped conjure Antique (a code review interface), a code search tool, and a source control IAM system. The decentralized approach embodied by Git is the right one for most code repos, according to Anthropic. But the company's main branch weighs in at about 100 GB, with a compressed working copy at more than a quarter of that. "We perform on the order of 25 million code checkouts per day for CI, before counting developer environments, agent sandboxes, and research jobs," Anthropic said. "Fetched naively, that would be over 600 PB of git traffic per day." Even with the tools Git provides for working with portions of a codebase, Anthropic says operations proved challenging. Scion has been designed to meet the needs of AI agents, so the client leaves much of the work to the server; the source control queries are exposed via API so internal tools can respond without needing a local repo, and there's less synchronization but more need for server speed. "In Scion, the unit of work is a 'changeset,' an entry in a write-ahead log," Anthropic explains. "A changeset stores most of what you’d expect from a commit in git. But where a git commit stores a pointer to the tree, a changeset stores a list of the files that changed relative to its first parent, along with content-addressed pointers to the compressed file contents in blob storage." Work on Scion started in January, and when Claude Mythos Preview became available internally, Anthropic's code coaxers told the model to rewrite an early Git-to-Scion ingestion pipeline. The much-hyped model produced a version that used 20 times less memory and ran four times as fast. When cost is no object thanks to ample venture funding, that sort of token spending just makes sense. Anthropic's Claude jockeys appear to be taking their obsolescence in stride. According to the AI biz, company developers who worked on Scion agree that Claude writes better code than they do. But they still possess a higher-level understanding that gives them a role as naysayers. "Very often, we found that the role of the engineers was to tell Claude 'no,'" Anthropic said. "Agents will sometimes violate core system constraints to satisfy a pattern that should never have been allowed in the first place." "Just say no." As a slogan, it's timeless. And it's never been more relevant. Anthropic says its bespoke system isn't right for general use. There will be no open source release. Nonetheless, the company contends that its own code scaling problems will become commonplace in other organizations over the next few months, so it wanted to share its approach – having ample funding to pay for writing custom infrastructure tools. ®

articles.headline: Can Vibe Coded Apps Replace Adobe and Microsoft? These AI Apps Hope So
keyFacts: Software engineer Brandon Thomas released 13 free, open-source apps designed to replicate core features of Adobe and Microsoft programs.
These apps offer alternatives to expensive subscriptions, though a CNET expert warned that sharing vibe-coded tools can create legal challenges.
Under a federal settlement agreement, Adobe will pay a $75 million civil penalty and provide $75 million in services to affected users.
body: In this current era of vibe coding — using AI to create mobile and desktop apps — it was probably only a matter of time until someone made free versions of popular apps. That happened this month when a Reddit user announced that he did so with popular but expensive Adobe and Microsoft programs.

The person behind the project is Brandon Thomas, a software engineer who uses the handle “u/ai_art_is_art” on Reddit, where the tools first caught AI enthusiasts’ attention. Thomas has released 13 free, open-source apps on his website, called ArtCraft. These apps aim to replicate the core functionalities of Adobe and Microsoft programs, including Photoshop, Word and PowerPoint — or, as Thomas calls them, PhotoCraft, WordCraft and DeckCraft.

Vibe coding has taken off for software developers and AI enthusiasts, leading to AI-made apps flooding Apple and Google’s app stores. However, significant concerns persist about the overall usefulness, security and long-term viability of vibe-coded apps. Apple removed some apps that help people vibe code this year because the apps didn’t comply with Apple’s developer rules.
More from CNET

But in the US’s current affordability crisis — and with legacy tech companies constantly raising their prices — a cheaper, AI-created alternative to Photoshop or Microsoft Word can be an attractive option for a subscription-weary consumer.

This certainly isn’t the first time a startup has tried to compete with legacy software companies like Adobe and Microsoft. Canva, Affinity and CapCut are extremely popular Adobe alternatives for content creation and editing. Google and Apple each have their own versions of Microsoft’s core business apps.

But ArtCraft’s vibe-coded apps and other potential AI-made apps allow individual users to avoid handing over their cash and data to a major tech company. Using an open-source AI model on your own device, for example, gives you more control over your data than using a cloud-based app through a subscription.
As with all apps, CNET recommends you inspect the privacy and safety policies before using them. This is especially important for vibe-coded apps.

“Vibe coding can make it super easy to swap out old software tools, but it’s legally questionable,” said CNET’s Blake Stimac, a vibe coding expert. “What works great for you as a quick fix could easily turn into a legal battlefield the second you try to share it with the world.”
Representatives for ArtCraft and Adobe did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Microsoft declined to comment.
Will vibe coding kill legacy software?

It’s unlikely that vibe-coded apps will be the sole downfall of legacy software companies like Adobe and Microsoft. But they do highlight the growing frustration with those companies, particularly as subscriptions become even more expensive and their programs become bloated with AI features.

In March, Adobe reached a $150 million settlement with the US government to resolve a federal lawsuit alleging that the software giant trapped consumers in subscription plans with hidden fees and an intentionally convoluted cancellation process. Under the terms of the agreement, Adobe will pay a $75 million civil penalty and provide $75 million in free services to affected users, though the company continues to deny any wrongdoing.

Microsoft has embedded its Copilot AI throughout its software ecosystem, despite notable user backlash. While the company recently removed a few Windows AI features due to negative feedback, it is still plowing ahead with billions of dollars in AI development.

The appeal of ArtCraft and other open-source vibe-coded apps is their ability to let individuals customize programs and avoid hefty subscriptions. The pitch is tailor-made for tech enthusiasts: If you only need limited access to these programs and can set them up yourself for free, why would you pay for Adobe Creative Cloud or Microsoft Office?

But that certainly won’t be the case for everyone. For one, many folks won’t want to take the time to figure out how to download and configure an open-source AI app. Meanwhile, businesses and professional creators will likely prefer the safety and privacy guarantees that Adobe and Microsoft offer, even if they aren’t always ironclad. Better the devil you know…

articles.headline: Apple’s HomeView ad is confusing to everyone except parents
keyFacts: Apple released an advertisement for its new HomeView smart display that depicts a chaotic morning routine for a family of five.
While tech analyst Benedict Evans found the ad stressful, parents and editor Bridget Carey described it as an accurate depiction of real mornings.
The device's real test will happen when it enters households to determine whether families use the shared display instead of individual phones.
body: Apple’s ad introducing its new HomeView smart display is a little unusual. It’s fast-paced and unruly, depicting a family of five as they rush through the morning routine. There’s yelling and mess, misplaced keys and discarded eggshells. Apple’s typical vibe is clean, simple, orderly; this commercial is chaos.
Apple’s HomeView ad is confusing to everyone except parents
The chaos is surprisingly real for an Apple commercial.
But the spot has parents — those with teen children in particular — feeling seen.

I’ll admit that it stressed me out the first time I watched it, too. Mornings getting my five-year-old out the door are a special breed of chaos, and usually culminate in us playing whatever ad-libbed game will get him to put his shoes on. But it’s not quite as intense as this one, which features dad making French toast, mom losing and finding keys in her pocket, a proxy battle over the thermostat, a teenage boy helping himself to whipped cream from a can, and an unexpected video call. There’s also a microdrama about the daughter’s ride to school with a boyfriend nobody knew about that ends with everyone gathered around the HomeView watching the security camera feed of the two of them departing the porch. It’s a lot for just over three minutes of screentime.

If I know anything, though, I know to trust my colleague Jen Tuohy, senior reviewer and parent to two teens, on matters of the home. Her take? “The most unrealistic part of the video is that no one is holding an iPhone.”

Other parents of teens shared similar reactions on Threads. When tech analyst Benedict Evans posted about the ad feeling stressful and confusing, CNET editor at large Bridget Carey chimed in to defend it, saying “It was exactly what my morning is like and it was the most real ad I’ve ever seen from Apple.” Others agreed, saying it “accurately captured” real life and that it “hit home,” no pun intended, at least I think.

Even if Apple didn’t need to do much to heighten the stakes of a family getting out the door, there is of course plenty of sleight of hand at work when it comes to making the HomeView appear so essential. The family has seemingly drilled a hole directly into the middle of their kitchen island to accommodate the charging cable, for one. And what sibling is going to check a text message from a secret boyfriend on the communal kitchen screen with their brother sitting at arm’s length? I don’t believe any teenager trusts Apple’s privacy features that far.

The confusion about the commercial is understandable. This is a far cry from the quiet luxury lifestyle everyone seems to enjoy in Apple’s Vision Pro ads. There’s also Evans’ observation that the HomeView doesn’t really solve any of the problems that come up throughout the course of the video. In the case of a spontaneous FaceTime call from the grandparents, the screen in the middle of the kitchen seems to make things worse.

But maybe morning chaos isn’t the problem that’s being solved. If the alternative is five people all interacting with their own phones, then the HomeView presents a different picture where everyone gets the essential information they need from one shared screen and stays more present.

A screen that makes you be more present is a lovely idea, but the real test will come when it’s in real households. Is the HomeView going to be enough to convince families to put their personal devices down? Will everyone just ignore it and keep scrolling on their own iPhones? These are questions worth answering before you start drilling holes in your kitchen island! In any case, an ungovernable morning routine is probably a feature of a busy household, not a bug. Just ask a parent.

articles.headline: Harry Kane overtakes Lionel Messi in stunning Champions League feat as he chases Cristiano Ronaldo streak
keyFacts: Bayern Munich striker Harry Kane scored twice in a 3-3 draw against Viking, surpassing Lionel Messi's record of Champions League goals scored after the age of 30.
Kane has now scored in nine successive games, putting him in a position to potentially chase Cristiano Ronaldo's record of 11 consecutive goals.
Bayern Munich sporting director Christoph Freund stated that contract extension discussions with Kane are going well and he feels comfortable at the club.
body: Harry Kane has impressively overtaken Lionel Messi for Champions League goals scored over the age of 30 in fewer games.
The striker netted twice in Bayern Munich ’s entertaining 3-3 draw at Norwegian side Viking on Tuesday evening.
Harry Kane fired scored twice for Bayern in a 3-3 draw against Viking and moved past Messi’s tally for Champions League goals after 30 Getty
Trailing 2-0 at the interval, Kane inspired Bayern to a comeback, scoring twice while playing a key role in his side’s third before they unfortunately conceded late on.
Kane’s first came from the penalty spot in the 54th minute and the England captain only had to wait a further six minutes to grab his second of the evening.
And it was that goal that took his tally to 36 goals in 40 games after the age of 30.
Kane, now 33, has bolstered his account since arriving in Bavaria in 2023, so much so that he has now eclipsed Messi ’s total.
The Argentine netted 35 goals in 48 games beyond his 30th birthday.
That shows the magnitude of Kane’s prowess in recent years while providing a ringing endorsement for his recent Ballon d’Or nomination .
Kane’s double means he has now scored for nine successive games to equal Robert Lewandowski and Ruud van Nistelrooy ‘s record.
And now Cristiano Ronaldo ’s record of 11 goals in succession is firmly in his sights ahead of the visit of Arsenal to the Allianz Arena next week, live on talkSPORT.
Should get on the scoresheet against the Gunners, Kane’s opportunity to equal Rona l do will come in the trip to Atletico Madrid next month.
Kane’s season at a glance
The striker is now up to eight goals for the season while registering four assists in his nine appearances.
Kane has now surpassed Messi’s tally and is also chasing Cristiano Ronaldo’s record
He is also now eyeing Ronaldo’s feat of 11 consecutive goals after scoring in his ninth straight European game Getty
Kane kicked off the season in style with three goals and three assists in five first five Bundesliga outings.
His brilliance has spilled onto the international scene with Kane having achieved his 125th cap for England, matching Peter Shilton ‘s all-time national appearance record.
He scored six times in England’s four matches during the recent international break, taking his tally to 91 goals for the Three Lions.
Kane’s contract with Bayern expires next summer but negotiations are on going over a two-year extension .
Bayern Munich sporting director Christoph Freund said on Friday that he is ‘very positive’ about discussions with Kane who himself has expressed his desire to remain at the club.
“There are always scenarios as long as it’s not signed,” Freund said. “There’s no new development.
Kane’s goals fired Bayern to a league and cup double as he scored 61 times for the club last season Getty
“The talks are going well. We’re very positive, everyone knows we’re determined to extend his contract and Harry feels very comfortable here.”
Since his arrival from Tottenham, Kane has scored an incredible 156 goals in 154 appearances.
He has scooped the Bundesliga Golden Boot in each of his three seasons, whilst firing Bayern to two Bundesliga titles.

articles.headline: Famous And Innovative Duke Nukem, Quake Level Designer ‘Levelord’ Has Died
keyFacts: Video game level designer Richard Gray, known as Levelord, has reportedly died at age 68.
Gray created popular maps for games including Duke Nukem 3D, Quake, and Sin, and co-founded Ritual Entertainment.
Colleagues and companies like Apogee Entertainment paid tribute to Gray following his passing.
body: Richard ‘Levelord’ Gray has reportedly died, according to Apogee Entertainment and individuals who were close to the legendary and beloved level designer who helped create fan-favorite maps in games like Duke Nukem 3D, Quake, and Sin.

Gray, known online by his mapping handle Levelord, explained in a 2016 interview that he didn’t really start making maps in games like Doom until he was 35. He later joined the Duke Nukem 3D team in his 40s, relatively late compared to most other game devs working on shooters in the ’90s and early 2000s. After that, he left and formed his own studio, which would eventually become Ritual Entertainment. That team worked on Quake’s first mission pack, Scourge of Armagon, Sin, Star Trek: Elite Force 2, and Counter-Strike: Condition Zero, among other games.

While working on the Quake mission pack at Ritual, Gray created “The Edge of Oblivion,” the third and last secret level of Scourge of Armagon. This level is credited by many as being the first “islands in space” or “platform in the void” type of FPS map. That style of map would become extremely popular in later FPS games like Unreal Tournament and Quake 3 Arena. Levelord also designed the MP map “Behind Zee Bookcase” in Sin, which is often credited as one of the first examples of a 3D FPS level designed to make you feel like you were the size of a small mouse exploring a real-world environment.

And of course, during his time developing levels in Duke Nukem 3D, he became famous for his hidden Easter egg messages tucked away in a part of the map that you could only reach using cheats. If you did, you’d find a message from Levelord: “You’re not supposed to be here.”
In 2016, when asked how he could be sure that players would even find the now-famous secret, Gray told Duke64Nukem.com:

Did we give you the cheat codes to find easily? Then, of course, most all of you would be flying around, seeing what you could break, find easter eggs the easy way â¦bingo! I gave you an easter egg that you had to cheat to find.
On Tuesday, devs who worked with Gray posted about the legendary developer in the wake of his passing.

“Devastating news today,” shared Doom co-creator and developer John Romero. “Richard ‘Levelord’ Gray was such a great guy. Like many of our friends, I wish I could have hung out with him again. He was full of life, a gentle soul, and an excellent level designer. He was called ‘Levelord’ for a reason.”
We are deeply saddened by the passing of Richard âLevelordâ Gray.
From his legendary work on Duke Nukem 3D to the countless players and developers he inspired, Richard leaves behind a lasting legacy.
Rest in peace, Levelord. pic.twitter.com/UZPWoM04XY
— Apogee Entertainment (@Apogee_Ent) October 13, 2026

“A heartbreaking day. Richard was a stellar talent who joined the game industry in his 40s when Apogee hired him to join the Duke 3D team,” posted Apogee founder Scott Miller. “He was a relentless hard worker, a fun teammate, and an overall great human. His levels in Duke Nukem 3D and Sin will live on forever. And Richard created one of the best easter eggs in gaming history: ‘You’re not supposed to be here! — Levelord.’ RIP.”

Fellow 3D Realms/Apogee Software developer Joe Siegler explained on social media that he heard the news from Gray’s wife and mentioned that the level designer had dealt with cancer over the years, though no cause of death has been officially confirmed yet.

“We worked together back at Apogee/3DR for a few years mostly on Duke Nukem 3D,” said Siegler. “Such a fun time in my life. We stayed in touch long after he left to found Ritual. Many dinners together with local crew. So many memories. So sad from this, but I know what cancer does. Much love to the Gray family”
Gray leaves behind a wife and daughter. He was 68 years old.

articles.headline: Send in the Clown is a turn-based RPG comedy about fighting one annoying child at a birthday party where there's only one fight in the whole game
keyFacts: Send in the Clown is a turn-based RPG comedy where players control a clown named Pockets to save a birthday party.
Players must befriend party guests through minigames to recruit them for a single battle against an annoying child named Tad.
The game is approximately one hour long, features a demo on Steam, and does not use artificial intelligence.
body: I generally find it quite frustrating how limited the medium of games insists on being when it comes to engaging in a wide breadth of genres. One particular genre that its filmmaking cousin frequently utilises but is rarely seen within games is comedy. Sure, occasionally a game makes an attempt at telling a joke within a cutscene (failing more often than not (comedy's hard!)), but rarely is it a genre mechanically. So I'm quite pleased to learn of Send in the Clown, a turn-based RPG where you play as a clown that has to save a 12 year old's birthday party… and it only has one turn.

In Send in the Clown, you play as Pockets, a horrendously sad name for a clown. He has been hired to perform at Miranda's birthday party, except it's being ruined by her shitty brother Tad. Your goal, then, is to save the day by saving the party by, uh, fighting a child! That's Tad, to be clear. The problem is, Tad is a dirty trickster, and despite you being a literal adult, isn't easy to take down. Your solution to that is by trying to make friends with everyone and anyone at the party.

That involves playing a range of minigames. There's a single dad who wants to impress with his dance moves but has two left feet, so you teach him through a rhythm game. There's an exhausted mum who you help give a "much-needed break from parenting with Uncharted-style quick time events." And there's an awkward shy kid who you have to hype up a bit to get him involved. After befriending them, they essentially get added to your party (the RPG kind) and can be used to take down Tad; I'm particularly fond of the mum's incredibly powerful attack where she throws her newborn baby.

It's not just about making friends, there are a range of secrets to unlock and discover that can aid you in taking down Tad. Eventually all of this culminates in a single battle, and yes, an entire battle system was developed just for this one battle. That's commitment! It's just the bulk of the game is in the delightfully silly prep work you have to do. Best of all, it's not trying to outstay its welcome; the game is only an hour long, so it doesn't sound like any grinding will be necessary. I also greatly appreciate this note on the Steam page: "No artificial intelligence, or intelligence of any kind, was used in the making of this game."
If any of this sounds up your alley, you can try out a demo, or just shoot it a wishlist, on its Steam page.

articles.headline: The rise and fall of a MAGA princess
keyFacts: US Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle resigned on Tuesday after the White House asked for her resignation over corruption allegations.
The Wall Street Journal reported that Guilfoyle solicited funds from a donor in exchange for access to Trump officials and media figures.
Guilfoyle is a former Fox News personality and ex-fiancée of Donald Trump Jr., whom President Trump said was not family.
body: President Donald Trump and US Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle in the White House on March 26, 2026. | Aaron Schwartz/Bloomberg via Getty Images
This story appeared in The Logoff , a daily newsletter that helps you stay informed about the Trump administration without letting political news take over your life. Subscribe here .
Welcome to The Logoff: Donald Trump’s ambassador to Greece, Kimberly Guilfoyle, is out of a job after serious corruption allegations.

What happened? Guilfoyle resigned on Tuesday after being shown the door earlier in the day by Trump’s brand-new White House press secretary, who announced at a briefing that Guilfoyle had been asked to resign.

Her departure comes just six days after a bombshell Wall Street Journal story , which described Guilfoyle’s efforts to solicit money from a Trump donor, including $100,000 to pay down a credit card bill, in exchange for access to Trump officials and conservative media figures.
Guilfoyle also attempted to conceal those efforts: In one text to the donor, Eric Deters, she wrote, “What a nightmare you’ll literally cost me my ambassadorship stop writing.”

Who is Guilfoyle? Fallen MAGA royalty. Guilfoyle, a former Fox News personality, is also the ex-fiancée of Trump’s eldest son, Donald Trump Jr. (and, more distantly, the ex-wife of current California Gov. Gavin Newsom, a Democrat).

There appears to be little love lost between Guilfoyle and Trump, however. On Tuesday, he told reporters that Guilfoyle “wasn’t a member of my family. She I guess dated my son a long time ago.” (The Don Jr.-Guilfoyle relationship is thought to have ended in 2024.)

Why was she forced out? Corruption allegations are not, generally speaking, dealbreakers in Trumpworld; the president and his children are all innovators when it comes to profiting off the presidency , and there’s plenty of self-dealing going on around them.

That being said, Guilfoyle may have crossed the line in two specific ways: one, her alleged corruption benefited her and not the Trump family. And two, the allegations are embarrassingly unsubtle even by the standards of the second Trump administration. The combination appears to have been too much.
And with that, it’s time to log off…

articles.headline: How will a diesel deal with Russia impact the U.S. market?
keyFacts: President Trump announced a deal for Russia to release 300,000 tons of diesel to U.S. and global markets.
Analysts stated that the amount is very small compared to U.S. consumption and will likely not lower prices significantly.
Analysts noted that Ukrainian strikes and sanctions have reduced Russia's refining capacity and export ability.
body: How will a diesel deal with Russia impact the U.S. market?
The price of diesel hit an all-time high in the U.S. in September. Can President Trump's deal for Russia to release more diesel onto the market bring the price down?
AILSA CHANG, HOST:

OK, there are plenty of legal and political questions surrounding President Trump's deal to get Russia to release more oil to the U.S. and global markets. And, of course, a lot of Americans are wondering how that deal could affect the price of diesel. NPR energy reporter Willa Rubin joins us now to talk about all of this. Hi, Willa.
WILLA RUBIN, BYLINE: Hi, Ailsa.
CHANG: Hi. OK, so give us the lay of the land here. What is happening with the price of diesel in the U.S. right now?

RUBIN: Well, it hit an all-time high a few weeks ago, which is important for the U.S. economy. You know, our industrial supply chain relies on diesel, tractors that farmers use, trucks that bring your food from farms eventually to the grocery store. If diesel is expensive, that contributes to the price of everything that you buy. Now, the price of a gallon has come down a little bit since that September high. On average, it's now $6.27, according to AAA, but that is still really high. Diesel is about $2.60 more than this time last year.
CHANG: OK, and explain this to me. What did President Trump say about how he expects this deal would work exactly?

RUBIN: Yeah, so in a post on Truth Social on Friday, President Trump said that Russia had agreed to release 300,000 tons of diesel to the U.S. and to global markets immediately. But, like, is that a little or a lot in terms of how much the U.S. actually uses?
CHANG: Yeah, which is it?
RUBIN: Yeah. So to put this in context for the rest of October, Will O'Neil is an analyst at S&P Global Energy. He's a follower of all things diesel.
WILL O'NEIL: Because I could even do some quick Excel math. So 300,000 tons over the course of 20 days is...
RUBIN: I love that you broke out an Excel spreadsheet mid conversation (laughter).
O'NEIL: That's what I do. That's my job.

RUBIN: So he figured out that if you convert tons to barrels and the U.S. uses up to 4 million barrels a day, the entire amount expected to be released in October adds up to about half the diesel the U.S. uses in just one day.
O'NEIL: It's drops in the bucket.
RUBIN: Drops in the bucket. And if you do some more math using the entire amount expected to be released over the coming months, O'Neil said it adds up to about nine days' worth.
CHANG: Let me ask you this. Is Russia really in any position to export all of this diesel?
RUBIN: Analysts in the U.S. don't know, but what...
CHANG: OK.
RUBIN: ...They do know is that Russia's refinery capacity has been significantly reduced by Ukraine's strikes. O'Neil says it's probably reduced 40- to 45% of their capacity.
O'NEIL: Ukrainian drone strikes have taken so much of its refining capacity offline that it just simply doesn't have the diesel production to send to global markets.

RUBIN: He says this deal does not change that reality. Russia has had an export ban since July, though they partially lifted it on Saturday. Also worth noting, the U.S. has had wide ranging sanctions on Russian energy since its full scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. On Friday, the Treasury Department announced it was temporarily waiving sanctions on diesel for about six months. And this has gotten some pushback from members of Congress on both sides of the aisle. This is a really complicated situation, Ailsa, with a lot of moving parts.
CHANG: Clearly. OK, if Russia really can bring this diesel to market, could that help lower prices in the U.S., you think, eventually?

RUBIN: Big picture, what drives diesel prices is global demand. And there's a global diesel deficit right now. A good chunk of that is due to the war in Iran. Claudio Galimberti is a partner and chief economist at Rystad Energy. He says the world is missing up to 1.5 million barrels per day that normally come from the Middle East and another million barrels that would come from Russia.
CLAUDIO GALIMBERTI: So it's a huge gap, and this deal only address (ph) a very small portion of that.
CHANG: OK, Willa, I'm no economist, but it sounds like he doesn't think this will really lower prices all that much. Am I getting that right?
RUBIN: Yeah. Analysts told me we will only start to see big meaningful drops in prices by solving these bottlenecks by ending the wars.
CHANG: That is NPR's Willa Rubin. Thank you so much, Willa.
RUBIN: Thank you so much, Ailsa.

articles.headline: Hideo Kojima Reviews The Resident Evil Movie
keyFacts: Writer-director Hideo Kojima reviewed Zach Cregger's Resident Evil movie, stating he was impressed by its horror techniques and experience reminiscent of playing the original game.
The Resident Evil movie has earned over $320 million worldwide, becoming the highest-grossing entry in the film series to date, according to the article.
Director Zach Cregger stated he has ideas for another Resident Evil movie, but plans to direct an original film titled The Flood next.
body: Writer-director Hideo Kojima has seen Zach Cregger's Resident Evil movie, and he has now shared his review. Kojima, a true cinephile known for his public movie reviews , said he "wasn't particularly interested" in seeing the movie at first, but he did, and he sounded pretty impressed by what he saw.

"Right from the opening, it hits you with music reminiscent of The Thing. From there, it’s a relentless barrage of classic horror techniques, terrifying situations, and jump scares that never lets up until the very end," he said .

Kojima went on to observe what others did as well, which is how the Resident Evil movie is more of a film that provides the "experience of playing Resident Evil" as opposed to watching an adaptation of one of its stories.

"It reminded me of how I felt when I first played the original Resident Evil on PlayStation back in 1996," he said. "I was just like [main character] Bryan in this movie. I kept getting game over after game over, shouting “F***!” over and over again. lol."
Austin Abrams as Bryan in the Resident Evil movie.

This is the kind of response that Cregger said he wanted viewers to have. It's also what got Cregger in some hot water with hardcore fans who wanted to see a straight adaptation of one of the games instead of Cregger's own original story set inside the world of Resident Evil.

Another bright spot for Kojima? While he was at the theater, he picked up some physical reading materials for the divisive new Tom Cruise movie Digger. A lot of people have had a lot of things to say about that film, and we are all waiting to hear what Kojima thought of it, whenever he sees it.

The new Resident Evil has made more than $320 million worldwide , following its big debut in China where it's made $40.7 million so far . Cregger's Resident Evil movie is now the highest-grossing entry in the series to date , surpassing the previous record-holder, which was 2016's The Final Chapter ($312 million).
For more, check out GameSpot's rundown of the highest-grossing Resident Evil movies of all time .
While Cregger has said he has ideas for another Resident Evil movie , he’s done with franchise movies and is instead making an original movie, The Flood, next .

As for Kojima, he's keeping very busy with the upcoming games OD and Phsyint , both of which are in the works for Xbox. Physint will also be adapted for film and TV , while Kojima's Death Stranding is coming to the big screen as well.
